White-breasted kingfishers (Halcyon smyrnensis) incubate their eggs for a period that has been documented under controlled conditions maintained at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], with hatching occurring after 19.5 days [ab = 19.5 days]. This incubation duration, derived from comparative data on the closely related belted kingfisher (Megaceryle alcyon), aligns well with the developmental pace expected for a medium-sized coraciiform bird. Newly hatched nestlings emerge at a modest wet weight of approximately 14.7 grams [Wwb = approximately 14.7 grams], a value that reflects the altricial condition typical of kingfishers, where neonates are initially blind, nearly naked, and entirely dependent on parental brooding and provisioning. This neonatal mass represents roughly 16 percent of the ultimate adult body mass recorded for the species. The thermal environment during incubation appears critical, as deviations from this optimal temperature can substantially extend or shorten the developmental window, influencing not only hatching success but also the initial condition of the chick upon emergence.

As the nestling period progresses, the chicks undergo rapid somatic growth, ultimately attaining an asymptotic body mass that defines the adult form. The ultimate wet weight for White-breasted kingfishers has been measured at approximately 91.4 grams [Wwi = approximately 91.4 grams], though previously published accounts such as those in the Animal Diversity Web report a typical adult range of 65.5 to 81 grams, suggesting that some variation exists across populations or between sexes. This species, belonging to the family Alcedinidae, exhibits a body size that places it among the larger members of the genus Halcyon, with a robust build suited to its piscivorous and carnivorous diet. Adults are characterized by a striking plumage combination of a rich chestnut head and breast, bright azure wings and tail, and a vivid white throat and belly, a coloration that is conspicuous during their characteristic perching and hunting bouts near freshwater wetlands, rice paddies, and coastal lagoons across their extensive range from the Middle East through South and Southeast Asia.

The reproductive biology of Halcyon smyrnensis has been modeled using life-history parameters derived from related species. Under standard thermal conditions reflective of the active breeding season at 40 °C [T = 40 °C], the time since birth at fledging is 21 days [tx = 21 days], a comparatively brief nestling phase that is typical of many tropical kingfishers and may be an adaptation to reduce predation risk in open nest cavities. Following fledging, the young birds attain puberty at 63 days since birth [tp = 63 days since birth], a value that is considerably later than the 18 to 20 days suggested by some sources, indicating that gonadal maturation may be delayed well beyond the period of physical independence at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This extended interval between fledging and reproductive competence likely reflects the time required for juvenile birds to develop proficient hunting skills, establish a territory, and accumulate sufficient body condition to support the energetic demands of nesting and chick rearing.

The maximum lifespan of this species has been estimated to be approximately 5.5 years [am = approximately 5.5 years] under the ambient thermal conditions typical of its active metabolic periods, which correspond to an environmental temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This longevity figure is consistent with the general life-history syndrome observed among medium-sized coraciiform birds, which tend to exhibit moderate annual survival rates tempered by the risks associated with aerial foraging and nest predation. The first successful brood is typically produced at 365 days since birth [tR = 365 days since birth], indicating that most individuals do not breed until their second calendar year at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This deferral of reproduction aligns with the time required for a juvenile to complete its post-fledging development, secure a breeding territory, and form a pair bond, all of which are prerequisites for successful nesting in the kingfisher social system.

In terms of annual reproductive output, females typically lay between 5 and 8 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 5 and 8 eggs per clutch], producing a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year] during a defined breeding season that corresponds to favorable prey availability. This reproductive strategy, which results in a relatively modest maximum daily rate of reproduction, is characteristic of a K-selected life-history approach where parental investment per offspring is high. Both parents participate actively in excavating the nest tunnel, incubating the eggs, and provisioning the growing chicks with small fish, crustaceans, and insects captured from nearby aquatic habitats. The combination of a limited clutch size and a single annual breeding attempt underscores the importance of each reproductive event for population recruitment, making the species particularly sensitive to habitat degradation and disturbance of its nesting banks during the breeding season.
